# Exam Hall Allocation System

Web application for allocating exam halls and seats, running the resit timetable from an
office-entered roster, and directing students and invigilators to their venues.

The project is a React + TypeScript single-page app backed by a Node/Express API and a
Supabase Postgres database, plus an optional Python service for crowding predictions.

---

## Requirements

| Tool | Version | Needed for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node.js | 20 or newer | frontend and API |
| npm | 10 or newer | installing dependencies |
| PostgreSQL | 14 or newer, or a Supabase project | the database |
| Python | 3.11 | optional ML crowding service |

---

## Install

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env      # then fill in the values, see below
```

---

## Configuration

`.env` is read by both Vite and the API. Values marked **required** have no sensible
default and the API will refuse to start without them.

### Required

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `SUPABASE_DB_URL` | Postgres connection string. On Supabase use the **session pooler** (port `5432`) and URL-encode the password. `DATABASE_URL` is accepted as an alias. |
| `JWT_SECRET` | Signs auth tokens. Generate one with `node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(64).toString('hex'))"`. |

### Usually set

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PORT` | `3002` | API port |
| `CLIENT_ORIGIN` | `http://localhost:5173` | CORS origin allowed to call the API |
| `VITE_API_URL` | `http://localhost:3002/api` | API base URL used by the browser |
| `APP_URL` | `http://localhost:5173` | absolute base URL used to build links in emails and notifications |

### Optional

The app runs fully without any of these; each only enables an extra capability.

| Variable | Effect when empty |
| --- | --- |
| `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT`, `SMTP_SECURE`, `SMTP_USER`, `SMTP_PASS`, `SMTP_FROM` | Password-reset emails are written to a simulated inbox instead of being sent. `SMTP_PASS` needs a 16-character Google App Password. |
| `VITE_GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` | Campus Locator uses free OpenStreetMap tiles, which need no billing account. |
| `SERP_API_KEY` | "Nearby places" search in the campus map is hidden. |
| `ML_SERVICE_URL`, `VITE_ML_SERVICE_URL` | Crowding predictions are unavailable and the UI hides them. |

> `VITE_`-prefixed variables are bundled into the browser code. Never put a secret in
> one. `SMTP_PASS` and `DATABASE_URL` are server-only and must not be prefixed with
> `VITE_`.

---

## Database setup

Schema changes are **numbered migrations** in `backend/migrations/`. They are applied in
order, each in its own transaction, and recorded in a `_migrations` table. Every
statement is idempotent, so running them against a database that already exists is safe
and only applies what is missing.

```bash
npm run db:migrate          # apply pending migrations
npm run db:migrate:status   # show applied / pending
npm run db:seed             # insert demo users, courses, halls, enrolments
npm run db:setup            # migrate + seed, for a new machine
```

Useful flags:

```bash
node backend/migrate.js --dry-run    # print statements without touching the database
node backend/migrate.js --force      # re-apply a migration whose file was edited
node backend/migrate.js --emit-schema  # regenerate backend/schema.sql
```

`backend/schema.sql` is a **generated** concatenation of the migration files, kept for
people who prefer to paste a schema into the Supabase SQL editor. Do not edit it by hand
— run `npm run db:schema`. A test fails if it drifts from the migrations.

To add a schema change, create the next numbered file in `backend/migrations/` and run
`npm run db:migrate`. Do not edit a migration that has already been applied; the runner
refuses to proceed if a recorded checksum no longer matches, unless you pass `--force`.

---

## The resit flow

A resit is not something a student asks for. The examinations office already knows who
is resitting, so the flow is **data entry first, scheduling second**, and the student
only ever reads the result.

```
office imports the roster  →  office places the students  →  everyone reads the timetable
      (pending)                    (scheduled)
```

There is no approval step. An imported row lands as `pending` and can be placed
immediately; `approved` still works for rows that predate the import path.

### Importing the roster

`POST /api/resit/requests/import` (admin only) takes rows of
`{ registration_number, course_code }` — one row per student and the course they are
sitting. Students and courses are **matched, never created**: a roster naming somebody
the system has never heard of is a list the office got wrong, not a request to enrol
them.

Rows that resolve commit; rows that do not come back in `problems` with the spreadsheet
line they were on, so a partly-wrong file still lands everything it got right. An
unexpected database error rolls the whole file back.

**The wizard shows its column mapping and lets the office correct it.** Headings are
guessed (`Index`/`Paper` will not be recognised, `Reg No` will), and every column is
listed with a dropdown of `registration_number`, `course_code`, `course_title` or
*ignore this column*. Changing one re-previews the rows immediately, so a department
whose spreadsheets call the same thing different names does not have to reformat the
file first. A field can only be filled from one column — pointing a second column at a
field already taken releases the first, so the wrong students can never be imported
silently. A sheet the parser did not recognise as a roster is still read as one, with
the same columns to check, rather than refused.

### What a placement is

**A resit placement is a hall, not a desk.** The `resit_seat_allocations` row per student
is what attendance is recorded against, but its `row_number`/`col_number` are `NULL`, as
are the segment's `row_start`/`row_end`/`col_start`/`col_end`. The invigilator works down
the roll by name and the student takes any free place. A legacy seated segment still
fills those columns and keeps its seat label.

A hall is therefore measured by `exam_capacity ?? total_capacity`, not by a desk grid —
a desk grid would let the office pack a hall to the last place on the last row.

**Scheduling is one transaction.** For every paper in the selected batch it will, or
will not, do all of:

1. reuse the active resit paper for the course, or create `<COURSE>-R1`;
2. register each student on that paper;
3. reuse the session for that date and time, or create it;
4. check the hall has room **for that sitting**;
5. create one **segment** — a paper sitting in one hall — and place each student;
6. recompute the segment's head count;
7. mark the requests `scheduled`.

A failure anywhere rolls the whole batch back, so a half-scheduled sitting cannot exist.

### How the timetable is shaped

- A **session** is a date and time (`resit_sessions`). Several papers share one.
- A **segment** is one paper in one hall for one session (`resit_session_papers`), and
  the invigilator staffing it.
- A **placement** is a student in a segment (`resit_seat_allocations`).

Two rules are worth knowing because they are easy to get wrong:

- **A hall is filled for a sitting, not for a day.** The same hall can host a morning and
  an afternoon resit. The capacity check is therefore scoped to the hall *and the start
  time* (`assertHallCapacity` matches the segment's `session_start`), so a hall used last
  week is free today.
- **Two papers can share a hall and a sitting.** They share the floor, not a place in it,
  so the second paper is not a double booking. Hall capacity is the constraint that keeps
  a shared sitting inside the room.

### Who can read and write what

| Audience | Endpoint | Sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admin | `GET /api/resit/timetable` | every session, every segment, every student |
| Invigilator | `GET /api/resit/timetable/mine` | only the segments they are staffing |
| Student | `GET /api/resit/my-seating` | only the placements they personally hold |

The invigilator scope is taken from the token, never the query, and it is applied to the
segment *and* placement queries — filtering only the session list would have handed each
invigilator a colleague's roster. The same scope gates
`POST /api/resit/timetable/segments/:id/attendance`, and it is checked against
`resit_session_papers.supervisor_id`, the same field the "mine" view uses, because a
session can be shared between papers while each segment still has one invigilator.

### Marking the roll

| Method | Endpoint | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One student | `POST /api/resit/timetable/segments/:segmentId/attendance` | admin, invigilator |
| The whole roll | `POST /api/resit/timetable/segments/:segmentId/attendance/bulk` | admin, invigilator |

Statuses are `present`, `absent` and `malpractice`, matching the column's CHECK. There
is no QR resit attendance: a student is found by name in a hall, not by scanning a
numbered desk, so the method is recorded as `manual` whatever the caller sends.

---

## Campus map and walking directions

A walking route is only as good as its two ends. The destination is an exam hall, whose
pin an administrator places on the map. The origin is the person, and that turned out to
be the weak end: the map used to fall back to an **IP location guess** whenever the phone
had no GPS fix, which is city-level — roughly ten kilometres. It never failed visibly, it
just produced a confident-looking route from the wrong place.

The rule now is that a wrong origin must be *visibly* wrong.

| Situation | Route starts from | What the person sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPS fix accurate to 100 m or better | the live position | nothing; it is simply their location |
| No fix, or a fix worse than 100 m | their saved start point | a banner saying the fallback is in use and why |
| No saved start point | the campus default (main gate) | a banner asking them to save a start point |
| Nothing known at all | no route | an explanation instead of a guess |

An IP fix is never used as a route origin. It is still used for one thing: noticing that
the device is tens of kilometres from campus, which is worth saying and useless for
routing.

**Arrival times are withheld when the origin cannot support one.** If the start point is
only accurate to 400 m and the walk is 120 m, "3 minutes" is noise, so no time is shown
instead. A saved landmark or pin is a known place and always supports a time.

### Placing pins

An administrator opens **Data Center → Campus Map Template** and places every hall and
landmark by clicking the map:

- **Halls** are moved with `PATCH /api/halls/:id/position`, which writes only the two
  coordinates. A mis-click cannot overwrite capacity, seating or the written directions.
- **Landmarks** are the named places people can start from — gates, hostels, car parks.
  Exactly one is the campus default (`uq_campus_landmarks_single_default` enforces it).
- **A pin outside the campus is refused** with a message saying how far out it was. A pin
  in the wrong place is worse than no pin, because it produces a confident wrong answer.

Removing a landmark goes to the **recycle bin**, not straight to deletion, so a pin
somebody depends on can be restored.

### Saving a start point

Each person saves one start point, in the map panel or by map view: a named landmark, a
pin of their own, or nothing. It is meant to be set once in a place with signal rather
than repeatedly during a walk through a building. Coordinates are stored on the user
alongside the landmark id, so a route can still be drawn if the landmark is later
recycled — the UI then says so and asks them to pick a new one.

---

## Running

Three processes, each in its own terminal:

```bash
npm run dev        # frontend  → http://localhost:5173
npm run api        # API       → http://localhost:3002
npm run ml-service # optional  → http://localhost:8000
```

Check the API came up:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3002/api/health     # {"ok":true}
```

### Demo logins

Seeded by `npm run db:seed`:

| Registration number | Password | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ADMIN01` | `admin` | admin |
| `INV01` | `invig` | invigilator |
| `STU001` | `student` | student |

The seed refuses to finish if the stored password hashes do not match these, so a
successful `db:seed` means the documented credentials work.

---

## Verifying an install

```bash
npm test              # 928 tests, frontend and backend
npx tsc --noEmit      # type check
npm run build         # production bundle
```

`npm test` runs the whole suite from the repository root, backend tests included: the
`.mjs` files under `backend/__tests__/` import Vitest, so `node --test` will not load
them.

There is a live check for the resit timetable, which runs against a started API
and a real database and removes everything it created afterwards:

```bash
npm run api            # in one terminal
node e2e-resit.mjs     # in another
```

It walks the office's own flow — import a roster including rows that cannot resolve,
re-import it, place the entries in a hall, try to overfill that hall, let the invigilator
mark the roll, try to mark a colleague's sitting — and checks the student only ever sees a
hall and never a seat.

---

## Deploying

1. `npm ci && npm run build` — the build runs `tsc --noEmit` first, so a type error
   fails the build instead of shipping.
2. Serve `dist/` from a static host and proxy `/api` to the Express process. The
   frontend uses a client-side router, so configure a **SPA fallback** that rewrites
   unknown paths to `index.html` (e.g. nginx `try_files $uri /index.html`,
   Netlify `_redirects: /* /index.html 200`, or Vercel's `rewrites`). `server.js` is
   API-only and does not serve the SPA.
3. Run the API with `NODE_ENV=production`. In production `JWT_SECRET` is required
   (the process refuses to start without it) and the rate limiters are enabled.
   Set `CLIENT_ORIGIN` to the deployed frontend origin and `APP_URL` to the public
   URL so emailed links resolve.
4. Set `VITE_API_URL` at build time if the API is on another origin; leave it as
   `/api` when the static host proxies to the API on the same origin.

---

---

## Project layout

```
backend/
  server.js            Express app: routes, middleware, error handling
  db.js                Postgres pool
  migrate.js           versioned migration runner
  migrations/          numbered, idempotent SQL migrations
  schema.sql           generated from migrations/ — do not edit
  seed.js              demo users, courses, halls, enrolments
  controllers/         request handling
  services/            business logic
  middleware/          auth, validation, rate limiting
  __tests__/           API and schema tests
src/
  pages/               one file per screen
  components/          reusable UI
  lib/apiClient.ts     HTTP client for the API
  lib/mockApi.ts       browser data layer; falls back to localStorage
  lib/seedData.ts      demo data for the browser store

```

---

## How data is stored

This matters when reading the code, because the application is **mid-migration** from a
browser-first design to a server-backed one.

- The API exposes **126 routes**. The browser data layer (`src/lib/mockApi.ts`) offers
  roughly **150 operations**, of which a handful are server-backed — the resit request
  queue, the resit timetable and notifications. The rest read and write `localStorage` and
  are visible only in that browser.
- So halls, courses, enrolments, scheduling, attendance, and venues are still
  browser-local. Signing in on a second device shows different data for those areas.
  Resit requests, allocations, and notifications are shared through the database.
- `src/lib/mockApi.ts` tries the API first and falls back to the browser store, so the
  app keeps working offline. That fallback is why the local-only areas are not obvious
  from the UI.

Planned work, in order: migrate halls, academic setup, users/enrolment, then scheduling
to the API; then add recycle bins for deleted records; then UI and accessibility cleanup.

---

## Known limitations

- **Indoor directions are generated, not surveyed.** `src/lib/indoorGraph.ts` builds a
  corridor/stairwell graph procedurally from the hall list, so routes follow a plausible
  layout rather than real surveyed floor plans. The `campus_nodes` and `campus_edges`
  tables exist in the schema for stored floor plans, but nothing reads or writes them yet.
- **The production bundle is a single ~2.1 MB chunk.** It works but would load faster
  split by route.
- **Notifications link to their resit application through `client_key`, not a foreign
  key** — `notifications.related_application_id` is currently always null.
- **Offline login ships demo credentials in the bundle.** `src/lib/seedData.ts` contains
  bcrypt hashes for `ADMIN01`, `INV01` and `STU001`, and they end up in the built
  JavaScript. When the API is unreachable, `mockApi.login` verifies against that local
  snapshot and issues an offline token. The server still rejects bad credentials with a
  401, which is not retried locally — but anyone who can read the bundle can log in as
  the seeded admin *while the API is down*. This is what makes the "works offline"
  feature work. Before exposing a real deployment, remove the seeded users from
  `MOCK_DATA` or gate the offline fallback behind a build flag.
- **The resit timetable is read-only in the UI.** Scheduling writes the paper, session,
  segment and placement, and the office, invigilator and student all read that back, but
  there is no drag-and-drop or "move this paper to another hall" screen. The browser
  mirror still has the older bulk generator, which edits localStorage directly.
- **Resit attendance is a roll call, not a scan.** A resit segment carries
  `supervisor_id` and its placements carry `attendance_status`, and the invigilator
  dashboard marks a student present, absent or for malpractice one button at a time or
  a whole segment at once. It is deliberately not the main exam `LiveSeatGrid` path: a
  resit placement has no numbered desk to scan, so a QR flow would have nothing to read.
- The database connection uses Supabase's session pooler. The pool handles idle
  disconnects, but very high concurrency would want the transaction pooler or direct
  connections.

# ML Models

This directory stores trained model artifacts (`.pkl` files) generated by the
training pipeline. Models are **not committed to git** because they are
regenerated from data.

## How to train

```bash
npm run ml-train
```

This runs `training/train_all.py` and produces:

| File | Algorithm | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `attendance_model.pkl` | XGBoost | Predict student no-shows |
| `attendance_scaler.pkl` | StandardScaler | Feature scaling for attendance |
| `anomaly_model.pkl` | Isolation Forest | Detect anomalous behavior |
| `anomaly_scaler.pkl` | StandardScaler | Feature scaling for anomalies |
| `seating_weights.pkl` | Heuristic weights | Optimal seating constraint weights |

## Expected training data

Place CSV or JSON files in `training/data/`:

- `attendance.csv` — student attendance records
- `incidents.csv` — malpractice / incident reports
- `enrollments.csv` — student-course enrollments
- `schedules.csv` — exam schedule entries
- `halls.csv` — exam hall metadata
- `students.csv` — student profiles (department, gender)

See `training/train_all.py` for column specifications.

## Graceful fallback

When models are absent the ML service automatically falls back to rule-based
heuristics. The system works without training — models improve accuracy.

# Plan: Fix student timetable inconsistency (exams vs lectures)

## Problem statement recap
- A student can have e.g. 6 exam courses but only 2 visible lectures
- Exams must follow courses the student pursued in the programme according to curriculum rule
- Chose: show courses with no published lecture as "not scheduled" (don't invent slots)
- Chose curriculum rule: Programme + level + semester (with blank course semester treated as included)
- Root causes:
  - Lectures filtered by enrollment AND status != 'draft' AND not deleted; exams filtered by enrollment (published). Different scoping.
  - Enrollment created too broadly in many places (all courses in programme ignoring level/semester). 
  - Some lectures missing/draft/deleted
  - Imported students enrolled in every course in programme ignoring level/semester (mockApi bulkCreateStudents ~2719)
  - createCourse/bulkCreateCourses auto-enroll all students in that programme regardless of level/semester
  - Seed auto-enrollment does filter by programme + level (seedData ~928) but other code paths don't follow curriculum rule

## Solution
1. **Add curriculum helper** - Use `getActiveCurriculum` from academicCalendar (program + level derived from intake/batch + semester from anchor session). Courses with blank semester are treated as included (already done). 
2. **Fix enrollment creation to follow curriculum rule** - Only enroll students in courses matching their programme AND derived level AND matching semester (or course.semester blank).
3. **Fix exam/lecture readers to use curriculum-based scoping** - For students, get their curriculum courses (by program+level+semester). Then look up exams/lectures for those course IDs. Also need to handle resolution of student IDs.
4. **Update StudentDashboard "My Lectures"** - Show ALL curriculum courses. For each, if there's a published/non-deleted lecture scheduled, show it; else show "Lecture not scheduled" with course info. Show counts like "X/Y scheduled".
5. **Fix bulkCreateStudents enrollment logic** - Currently enrolls all courses in programme (ignoring level/semester). Should enroll only curriculum-matching courses.
6. **Fix createCourse/bulkCreateCourses** - Don't auto-enroll everyone in programme; enroll only students whose curriculum includes that course.
7. **Backend lecture service** - Also needs to align? The backend filters by enrollments; but problem says "scan through them all and fix that" - includes both frontend/mock and backend. Let us look up backend behavior again.

# ML Training Data Upload Guide

This guide explains how to upload and train ML models using CSV/Excel files for the exam hall allocation system.

## Overview

The ML Training feature allows administrators to:
1. Upload training data files (CSV/Excel)
2. Review uploaded data
3. Train AI models for:
   - **Attendance Prediction**: Predict student no-shows
   - **Anomaly Detection**: Detect suspicious behavior patterns
   - **Seating Weights**: Optimize seating constraints

## Accessing the ML Training Feature

1. Log in as an administrator
2. Navigate to the Admin Dashboard
3. Click on "ML Training" in the sidebar (purple gradient button)

## Step 1: Upload Files

### Required File Types

#### 1. Attendance Records (`attendance.csv/xlsx`)
**Purpose**: Student attendance data for training prediction models

**Required Columns**:
- `student_id`: Unique student identifier
- `exam_schedule_id`: Reference to exam schedule
- `attendance_status`: 'present', 'absent', 'malpractice'
- `check_in_time`: Timestamp when student checked in
- `start_time`: Exam start time
- `row_number`: Seating row position
- `col_number`: Seating column position

**Example CSV**:
```csv
student_id,exam_schedule_id,attendance_status,check_in_time,start_time,row_number,col_number
1,101,present,2026-10-13 08:45:00,2026-10-13 09:00:00,2,3
2,101,absent,,2026-10-13 09:00:00,,
3,101,present,2026-10-13 08:50:00,2026-10-13 09:00:00,3,1
```

#### 2. Incident Reports (`incidents.csv/xlsx`)
**Purpose**: Exam incident reports for anomaly detection

**Required Columns**:
- `student_id`: Student identifier
- `incident_type`: Type of incident (e.g., 'cheating', 'disturbance')
- `severity`: Severity level ('low', 'medium', 'high', 'critical')
- `timestamp`: When the incident occurred

**Example CSV**:
```csv
student_id,incident_type,severity,timestamp
5,cheating,high,2026-10-13 10:30:00
12,disturbance,low,2026-10-13 11:15:00
```

#### 3. Enrollments (`enrollments.csv/xlsx`)
**Purpose**: Student-course enrollment mappings

**Required Columns**:
- `student_id`: Student identifier
- `course_id`: Course identifier

**Example CSV**:
```csv
student_id,course_id
1,101
1,102
2,101
3,103
```

#### 4. Exam Schedules (`schedules.csv/xlsx`)
**Purpose**: Exam schedule data with halls and times

**Required Columns**:
- `id`: Schedule ID
- `course_id`: Course identifier
- `exam_hall_id`: Hall identifier
- `start_time`: Exam start time
- `end_time`: Exam end time

**Example CSV**:
```csv
id,course_id,exam_hall_id,start_time,end_time
101,201,1,2026-10-13 09:00:00,2026-10-13 11:00:00
102,202,2,2026-10-13 14:00:00,2026-10-13 16:00:00
```

#### 5. Exam Halls (`halls.csv/xlsx`)
**Purpose**: Hall capacity and facilities data

**Required Columns**:

**Requirements**: attendance, incidents files

**Requirements**: attendance, incidents files

## 1. Executive Summary & Introduction

### 1.1 Project Overview

The **AI-Driven Exam Hall Locator and Scheduler** is an integrated examination-management platform designed to replace fragmented, manual processes for planning examinations, allocating halls and seats, supervising attendance, and guiding students to their examination venues.

The system combines a responsive React frontend, a Node.js/Express API, a PostgreSQL database hosted through Supabase, and an optional Python FastAPI machine-learning service. It supports three primary user groups:

- **Students**, who view examination schedules, seat assignments, venue directions, resit information, attendance records, reminders, and academic-support features.
- **Invigilators**, who view assigned shifts, verify student identity through QR scanning or manual attendance, record incidents, and submit examination reports.
- **Administrators**, who manage halls, courses, enrolments, examination schedules, seat allocation, invigilator assignment, resit rosters, campus map pins, notifications, and system health.

The platform is designed as an offline-tolerant, mobile-ready application. It supports standard web deployment and native packaging through Capacitor for Android and iOS.

### 1.2 Background

University examination administration is operationally complex. Examination offices must coordinate:

- Course enrolments and student eligibility.
- Hall capacity, seating layout, laboratory requirements, and accessibility.
- Invigilator availability and workload limits.
- Examination timetables that avoid hall, invigilator, and student clashes.
- Student wayfinding across large campuses.
- Identity verification and attendance capture at examination venues.
- Resit registration, hall placement, and result communication.
- Real-time or near-real-time visibility for invigilators and administrators.

When these activities are handled with spreadsheets, paper lists, notice boards, and disconnected messaging, several recurring problems emerge:

- Students receive late or ambiguous venue information.
- Hall capacity is underused or exceeded.
- Invigilators are double-booked or assigned unevenly.
- Attendance records are inconsistent and difficult to audit.
- Students with overlapping examinations are identified too late.
- Resit administration becomes a separate, error-prone process.
- Campus navigation is difficult for new students and visitors.

The project addresses these problems by centralizing examination data, automating allocation decisions, providing digital wayfinding, and introducing verifiable QR-based attendance workflows.

### 1.3 Problem Statement

The institution requires a reliable, auditable, and user-friendly system that can answer the following questions accurately and quickly:

1. **When and where is each examination taking place?**
2. **Which hall and seat are assigned to each student?**
3. **How does a student navigate from their current location to the correct venue?**
4. **How can an invigilator verify that the person presenting an ID is the allocated student?**
5. **How can the examination office allocate many students without creating clashes?**
6. **How can resit candidates be imported, placed in halls, and tracked separately from main examinations?**
7. **How can administrators monitor data quality, system health, and operational exceptions?**

The system solves these questions through a single platform with role-specific dashboards, automated scheduling and seating logic, QR-based identity checks, and an interactive campus navigation interface.

### 1.4 Proposed Solution

The proposed solution is a modular, service-oriented application with the following high-level capabilities:

- **Centralized academic data management** for users, faculties, departments, courses, enrolments, halls, and examination slots.
- **Automated examination scheduling** using heuristic allocation and an optional genetic-algorithm optimizer.
- **Seat allocation** with configurable anti-cheating and accessibility strategies.
- **Campus mapping and route navigation** using OpenStreetMap data, OSRM walking routes, and an offline road-graph fallback.
- **Student identity verification** using permanent and time-limited QR payloads.
- **Attendance logging** through QR scan confirmation and manual or bulk invigilator updates.
- **Resit administration** through roster import, hall placement, timetable generation, and role-scoped visibility.
- **Student academic support** including revision timelines, deadline reminders, study groups, calendar events, and an AI study assistant.
- **Administrative governance** including soft deletion, recycle-bin restoration, notification delivery, audit data, and data-health checks.

### 1.5 Core Objectives

| Objective | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Automate allocation** | Reduce manual scheduling effort while maintaining clash-free timetables. |
| **Improve student experience** | Give students clear, mobile-friendly access to schedules, seats, directions, and reminders. |
| **Strengthen examination integrity** | Use QR identity checks, attendance status, incident notes, and audit metadata. |
| **Optimize venue utilization** | Match cohorts to hall capacity and support shared-hall examination sections. |
| **Support accessibility** | Provide accessible seating strategies, venue metadata, and accessible route preferences. |
| **Enable offline resilience** | Preserve critical student and operational views when connectivity is poor. |
| **Centralize resit operations** | Import, place, schedule, and track resit candidates without a separate spreadsheet workflow. |
| **Provide operational visibility** | Give administrators dashboards for schedules, allocations, map configuration, notifications, system health, and data recovery. |

### 1.6 Scope

#### In Scope

- Role-based authentication and authorization for students, invigilators, and administrators.
- Examination hall, course, enrolment, slot, and schedule management.
- Automated and manual examination scheduling.
- Seat allocation with multiple seating strategies.
- Shared-hall section planning for multiple courses.
- Campus map pins, landmark management, walking directions, indoor routing, and offline route fallback.
- QR generation, scanning, verification, attendance confirmation, and replay prevention.
- Invigilator attendance, incident, and examination-report workflows.
- Resit roster import, placement, timetable generation, attendance, and student visibility.
- Notifications, student reminders, academic calendar, study groups, revision planning, and AI study assistance.
- Soft-delete and recycle-bin restoration for selected administrative entities.
- Web deployment and Capacitor-based mobile packaging.

#### Out of Scope

- Real-time WebSocket or Socket.io event streaming. The current implementation uses REST request/response, polling, refresh, web push, and local notifications.
- Fully surveyed indoor floor plans. Indoor graphs are generated procedurally from hall metadata.
- Payment processing. The current resit workflow is office-driven and does not require student payment.
- Biometric identity verification. QR verification is the implemented identity mechanism.
- Automated invigilator payroll or full human-resource management.
- Formal accreditation or examination-board policy enforcement beyond system rules.

## 2. System Architecture & Tech Stack

### 2.1 Architectural Style

The system follows a **layered client-server architecture** with an optional machine-learning sidecar:

1. **Presentation layer** — React single-page application for web and Capacitor native shells.
2. **API layer** — Express REST API responsible for authentication, authorization, validation, business rules, and persistence.
3. **Data layer** — PostgreSQL, hosted locally or through Supabase, accessed directly by the API through the `pg` driver.
4. **Intelligence layer** — Optional FastAPI service for optimization, prediction, anomaly detection, and congestion analysis.
5. **Integration layer** — Email delivery, web push, OSRM routing, map tiles, and LLM-based study assistance.

The frontend is intentionally decoupled from the database. All privileged operations pass through the API, while selected browser-local features use a resilient data layer with localStorage fallback.

### 8.12 Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API exits immediately | `JWT_SECRET` missing in production | Set a strong secret. |
| API cannot connect to database | Invalid `SUPABASE_DB_URL`, SSL mode, or password encoding | Verify connection string and URL-encode special characters. |
| Port 3002 already in use | Another API process is running | Stop it or set `PORT=3003`. |
| Login fails for demo user | Seed not run or hash mismatch | Run `npm run db:seed`. |
| No hall routes shown | No map pins or no saved origin | Configure pins and save a start point. |
| OSRM route unavailable | Network/rate limit | Offline graph or distance estimate is used. |
| QR scanner cannot open camera | Browser permission or insecure origin | Use HTTPS/localhost and grant camera permission. |
| Dynamic QR rejected in production | `QR_NONCE_SECRET` missing or changed | Configure a stable secret. |
| Push notifications not delivered | VAPID keys or subscription missing | Configure VAPID and re-subscribe. |
| ML endpoints fail | Python service not running or model missing | Start the service and train models. |
| Schema drift | `schema.sql` edited manually | Regenerate with `npm run db:schema`. |
| Migration checksum mismatch | Applied migration edited | Revert the file or use `--force` intentionally. |
| SPA routes 404 in production | Missing fallback rewrite | Configure `try_files` or equivalent. |

### 8.13 Known Limitations and Future Work

#### Current Limitations

- **No WebSocket transport** — live views use request/response, polling, refresh, and push notifications rather than a persistent real-time channel.
- **Hybrid storage model** — some halls, courses, enrolments, and scheduling data remain browser-local while resit and notification data are server-backed.
- **Indoor plans are generated** — routes follow a plausible corridor/stair graph rather than surveyed floor plans.
- **Single production bundle** — the frontend is built as a large single chunk, which could be split by route for faster loading.
- **Offline demo credentials** — the local fallback includes seeded demo credentials in the bundle; this must be disabled or gated before a public production deployment.
- **Resit timetable editing** — the current UI is primarily read-oriented for generated resit timetables; advanced drag-and-drop hall reassignment is not implemented.
- **Resit attendance is manual** — resit placements may be hall-level rather than desk-level, so attendance is roll-call based.
- **Database pooling** — the session pooler is suitable for the current workload; very high concurrency may require a transaction pooler or direct connection strategy.

#### Recommended Future Enhancements

1. Migrate all browser-local domains to server-backed APIs.
2. Add a WebSocket or server-sent event channel for live attendance and operational dashboards.
3. Replace procedural indoor graphs with surveyed floor plans stored in `campus_nodes` and `campus_edges`.
4. Add drag-and-drop resit and examination rescheduling.
5. Implement route-level code splitting and bundle optimization.
6. Add comprehensive audit dashboards for schedule and attendance changes.
7. Add institution-wide role management and delegated permissions.
8. Add automated accessibility and performance regression tests.
9. Add multi-campus tenancy and campus-scoped configuration.
10. Remove or gate offline demo credentials before public deployment.

---

## Conclusion

The AI-Driven Exam Hall Locator and Scheduler provides a coherent, role-aware platform for examination planning, venue allocation, student wayfinding, QR identity verification, attendance capture, and resit administration. Its architecture separates the interactive client, transactional API, relational database, and optional machine-learning service while preserving graceful fallbacks when external intelligence or connectivity is unavailable.

The system’s strongest architectural qualities are its explicit role boundaries, transactional scheduling operations, layered constraints, QR replay prevention, and dual online/offline operating model. Its most important production considerations are the hybrid browser/server data model, the absence of WebSocket streaming, the need for strong secrets and production-only safeguards, and the requirement to remove demo credentials from public builds.

With the documented setup, migration, and deployment procedures, the project can be run locally for demonstration, evaluated academically, and extended toward a fully centralized, institution-wide examination management platform.

# Supabase setup

The API talks to Postgres directly. There is no Supabase JavaScript client in the
browser, so you only need a database connection string — not a project URL or anon key.

## 1. Create a project

Create a project at <https://supabase.com> and stay within the free plan.

## 2. Get the connection string

**Project Settings → Database → Connection string → Session pooler**.

Use the **session pooler** (port `5432`) rather than the transaction pooler (port
`6543`): the API holds a connection pool and issues session-scoped SQL. The direct
connection (`db.<ref>.supabase.co:5432`) also works.

Copy the string but **URL-encode the password** — Supabase passwords often contain
characters that must be escaped:

```
postgresql://postgres.PROJECT_REF:PASSWORD@aws-0-REGION.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres?sslmode=require
```

The pool handles the pooler dropping idle connections, but very high concurrency would
want direct connections.

## 3. Configure the environment

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

```env
SUPABASE_DB_URL=postgresql://postgres.PROJECT_REF:PASSWORD@aws-0-REGION.pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres?sslmode=require
JWT_SECRET=<generate with: node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(64).toString('hex'))">
```

The database password belongs only in `SUPABASE_DB_URL`. Never put it in a `VITE_`
variable, and never commit `.env`.

## 4. Create the schema and demo data

```bash
npm run db:migrate    # apply migrations in backend/migrations/
npm run db:seed       # demo users, courses, halls, enrolments
```

`npm run db:migrate:status` shows what has been applied. Re-running the migration is
safe — every statement is idempotent and applied migrations are recorded in a
`_migrations` table.

### Prefer the SQL editor?

`backend/schema.sql` is generated from the migration files and contains the same
statements in one file. Paste it into the SQL Editor and run it. Prefer the migration
runner where you can, because it records what it applied and stays in step with later
changes. Regenerate the file with `npm run db:schema`.

## 5. Run it

```bash
npm run api    # → http://localhost:3001
npm run dev    # → http://localhost:5173
```

Check the API is up and connected:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3001/api/health     # {"ok":true}
```

Sign in with `ADMIN01` / `admin` after seeding.

## What is actually stored in the database

Only part of the application is server-backed. Resit applications, payments, fees,
resit allocations, notifications, password resets and authentication live in Postgres.
Halls, courses, enrolments, timetables, attendance and venues are still stored in the
browser's `localStorage`, so they are per-device. See the "How data is stored" section
of the main `README.md` for the current split.

## Notifications

Notifications are delivered through the in-app notification centre and on-screen
banners. No email is sent for in-app notifications, and no email service configuration
is required. Email is only used for self-service password resets, and that falls back
to a simulated inbox when SMTP is not configured.
